standard.title: Citizens working for civic goals
standard.description: how citizens (members of communities) with shared beliefs and values work together to achieve a civic goal
standard.prior_knowledge: From AC9HS4K09 (Community identity and diversity): Students explain how communities are diverse and how people within communities have shared identities and belonging. Students understand that community groups serve different purposes.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain how citizens with shared beliefs and values work together to achieve a civic goal, giving examples of community groups that pursue shared goals and evaluating the importance of civic participation.

nodes.label: What is a civic goal?
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the concept of a civic goal — a shared aim that benefits a community or society — and distinguish civic goals from personal or commercial goals.
nodes.minimum_width: Define 'civic goal' and give one example of a community pursuing a civic goal.
nodes.typical_width: Explain what a civic goal is — an aim that benefits the broader community or society — and give examples of civic goals pursued by different types of community groups, distinguishing these from personal goals (benefiting an individual) or commercial goals (benefiting a business).
wider: Investigate the relationship between civic goals and democratic values — how do shared values motivate citizens to work together for community benefit?
Explore examples of civic goals at different scales: local (school/neighbourhood), regional, national and global, and compare the challenges of pursuing civic goals at each scale
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish civic goals from personal or commercial goals will describe community groups without understanding what makes their aims distinctively civic. This distinction is the conceptual foundation for understanding citizenship and collective action.

response_modes.reason: Use a three-column sorting framework (personal / commercial / civic) with real examples to make the distinction concrete before moving to analysis of how civic goals are pursued.

success_criteria: Students explain the meaning of 'civic goal' and distinguish it from personal or commercial goals.
Students give at least one example of a community pursuing a civic goal.

nodes.label: How citizens organise and work together
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how citizens with shared beliefs and values organise themselves into groups and work collectively to pursue civic goals, including through volunteering and community organisations.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe how one community group organises itself and works toward a civic goal.
nodes.typical_width: Explain how different types of community groups (religious and other charities, rural fire services, surf life-saving clubs, emergency services, First Nations community groups, youth groups) organise themselves around shared values and work collectively to achieve civic goals.
wider: Investigate a First Nations Australian community organisation and explain the services it provides, the values it is built around, and how it supports community goals
Examine how digital platforms and social media are used by citizens to organise around shared civic goals at local, national and global levels

response_modes.reason: The range of community group types in the elaborations is important — students benefit from seeing how civic organisation occurs across very different contexts, from emergency services to cultural organisations to digital advocacy.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: First Nations community organisations and the use of digital media for civic organising are two distinct and substantive wider directions in the elaborations — both extend the concept of civic participation beyond the conventional volunteer model.
success_criteria: Students describe how at least one community group is organised around shared values and goals.
Students explain at least two ways members of the group work together to pursue their civic goal.

nodes.label: Why citizens participate in civic life
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain why citizens choose to participate in civic life and community groups, including the connection between shared beliefs and values and the motivation to act for community benefit.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain two reasons why citizens might volunteer or participate in a civic organisation.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the motivations for civic participation: shared values and beliefs, concern for community wellbeing, cultural and religious obligation, desire to make a difference, and the social benefits of belonging to a community organisation.
wider: Survey members of a local community organisation to investigate their motivations for participation, and compare their responses with the elaboration examples
Explore how civic participation is connected to broader democratic values — making the link between individual participation and the health of democracy explicit

response_modes.reason: The link between values and motivation is an inferential move students may not make automatically — use examples that make the value-to-action pathway explicit (e.g. 'We believe in protecting life, so we volunteer with the SES').

success_criteria: Students explain at least two reasons citizens participate in civic organisations.
Students connect at least one motivating reason to a shared value or belief.

nodes.label: Evaluating civic participation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate the importance of civic participation in a democratic society, explaining how citizens working together for civic goals contributes to community wellbeing and democratic health.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain why civic participation is important in a democracy, using at least one example.
nodes.typical_width: Evaluate the importance of civic participation for community wellbeing and democracy, explaining how collective action around shared values achieves goals that individuals or governments acting alone cannot, and give examples from Australian and global contexts.
wider: Investigate how civic participation has changed over time in Australia (e.g. changes in volunteering rates, new forms of civic action) and evaluate what this means for the health of Australian democracy
Assess whether digital forms of civic participation (e.g. online petitions, social media campaigns) are as effective as traditional forms, and what each contributes differently to civic goals

response_modes.reason: Evaluation of civic participation connects the concept of civic goals, the mechanics of collective action, and the motivation of citizens into a single analytical judgment. Support students with a structured argument frame.

success_criteria: Students explain why civic participation matters for community wellbeing and democracy.
Students give at least one example of citizens working together to achieve a civic goal.
Students use relevant civic terms accurately (e.g. 'civic', 'volunteer', 'community organisation', 'shared values').
